clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive multisystem disorder caused by biallelic SMARCAL1 mutations; the classic triad is spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, T-cell immunodeficiency and steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome.
Disproportionate short stature with a short trunk; skeletal survey shows spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia with ovoid or flattened vertebral bodies and capital femoral epiphyseal (hip) dysplasia.
Progressive steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome due to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, typically advancing to end-stage kidney disease.
T-cell predominant immunodeficiency with lymphopenia predisposes to recurrent bacterial, viral, fungal and opportunistic infection.
Cerebrovascular disease — transient ischaemic attacks, migraine-like headache, a moyamoya-like arteriopathy and strokes — is a major source of morbidity.
Supportive features include hyperpigmented macules, fine sparse hair, characteristic facies (broad depressed nasal bridge with a bulbous nasal tip) and generalised, accelerated atherosclerosis.
Two overlapping severities exist — a severe infantile or antenatal-onset form and a milder later-onset (juvenile) form — broadly tracking residual SMARCAL1 function.
Bone marrow dysfunction and hypothyroidism may complicate the course, and live vaccines are hazardous given the underlying T-cell defect.
reference.pathophysiology: Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in SMARCAL1 on chromosome 2q35, which encodes an ATP-dependent annealing helicase (also termed HARP) of the SNF2 chromatin-remodelling family. SMARCAL1 is recruited to stalled DNA replication forks via replication protein A, where it stabilises and restarts forks and participates in replication-associated DNA repair and maintenance of genome integrity. Impaired annealing-helicase and chromatin-remodelling activity is thought to compromise fork restart and tissue-specific gene expression, producing a pleiotropic phenotype affecting chondrocytes (spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia), the developing immune system (defective T-lymphocyte production and lymphopenia), the glomerular podocyte (focal segmental glomerulosclerosis) and the vasculature (premature arteriopathy with cerebral ischaemia). Phenotype severity correlates broadly with the degree of residual enzyme function, and a minority of clinically typical patients lack a detectable SMARCAL1 mutation, implying additional loci or modifying factors.
additionalDifferentials: Severe infantile SIOD versus milder juvenile-onset SIOD (allelic severity spectrum within the same disorder)
Cartilage-hair hypoplasia (RMRP) — the other classic immuno-osseous dysplasia
Other spondyloepiphyseal dysplasias (e.g. COL2A1-related spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita)
Genetic steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome / focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (e.g. NPHS1, NPHS2, WT1-related)
Combined immunodeficiencies presenting with growth failure and recurrent infection
Progeroid or metabolic syndromes with disproportionate short stature and vascular disease
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey / radiographs demonstrating spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia (flattened ovoid vertebrae, capital femoral epiphyseal changes)
SMARCAL1 molecular genetic testing (sequencing with deletion/duplication analysis)
Urinalysis with quantitative proteinuria and renal biopsy (focal segmental glomerulosclerosis)
Lymphocyte subset enumeration and immunoglobulin levels (T-cell lymphopenia)
Full blood count and blood film to detect cytopenias and marrow dysfunction
Brain MRI with MR angiography for cerebral ischaemia and moyamoya-like vasculopathy
Thyroid function tests and fasting lipid profile
redFlags: Acute focal neurological deficit or seizure suggesting cerebral ischaemia or stroke
Opportunistic or overwhelming infection in a lymphopenic child
Rapidly progressive renal failure or an uncontrolled nephrotic state
Signs of bone marrow failure with severe cytopenias
reference.prognosis: The outlook is guarded, particularly in the severe infantile form where death in childhood from renal failure, infection, stroke or marrow failure is common. The juvenile form may survive into adulthood but with cumulative renal, immune and cerebrovascular morbidity.
pitfalls: Attributing steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome to common acquired causes and missing the underlying genetic diagnosis.
Overlooking the T-cell immunodeficiency and administering live vaccines.
Ascribing short stature to an isolated skeletal dysplasia without evaluating the renal and immune systems.
Underestimating cerebrovascular risk, so that stroke as a cause of neurological decline is not anticipated.
Assuming a negative SMARCAL1 result excludes the diagnosis when the phenotype is classic.
references: Inborn errors of immunity / primary immunodeficiency guidelines
management: No disease-specific therapy exists, so care is organ-directed; use RAAS blockade (ACE inhibitors or ARBs) to reduce proteinuria in the steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, recognising that immunosuppression is generally ineffective
Progress to kidney replacement therapy with dialysis and kidney transplantation for end-stage kidney disease from the focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

Manage the T-cell immunodeficiency with antimicrobial prophylaxis, immunoglobulin replacement, avoidance of live vaccines and prompt treatment of opportunistic infection, considering haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation in severe combined immune or marrow failure
Address the moyamoya-like cerebral arteriopathy with antiplatelet therapy and neurosurgical revascularisation where indicated, and treat migraine and transient ischaemic attacks
Reduce accelerated atherosclerotic risk with lipid-lowering therapy and blood-pressure control, and provide orthopaedic surveillance for the spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia and hip disease
Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary team spanning nephrology, immunology, neurology, orthopaedics and clinical genetics
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder with SMARCAL1 testing and screening of at-risk siblings
